title: Spare tempi
summary: Pawn endings: whoever has a pawn move to spare wins the zugzwang fight.
part.pass.title: One move to spare
part.pass.summary: When the side to move loses, a pawn move hands the move to the other side.
part.count.title: Counting tempi
part.count.summary: Both sides have pawn moves: whoever has more wins.
part.double.title: One step or two
part.double.summary: A pawn on its starting square can give two tempi, if it moves one square at a time.
part.timing.title: At the right moment
part.timing.summary: First the king takes its post; the spare tempo is kept for the end.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Three rules to keep and an ending to play.
step.t_pass: White to move. Each king attacks the other pawn and defends its own. Whoever steps away gives up his pawn. What does White do here?
step.t_pass.hint1: Picture the position without the h2-pawn. Whoever had the move would be lost. So you want Black to be the one moving.
step.t_pass.hint2: There is a white piece that can move without spoiling anything in the centre.
step.treb: A reminder from the mined-squares lesson: without the h-pawns, this position is the trébuchet. Each king attacks the other pawn, and whoever has the move loses.
step.spare: Now put the h2-pawn back. It attacks nothing, defends nothing and is far from everything. Still, it decides the game: h3 or h4 changes nothing in the centre and hands the move to Black. A move like that is called a spare tempo. In a pawn ending it can be worth as much as an extra pawn.
step.d_pass: Watch what happens when Black gets the move.
step.d_pass.m1: h3. The waiting move. The centre stays the same, but now Black has to move.
step.d_pass.m2: The black king has no good square: every move drops the d5-pawn or stops attacking d4.
step.d_pass.m3: Kxd5. The pawn falls, and my king still guards the d4-pawn.
step.d_pass.m4: The black king attacks d4, but the pawn is protected.
step.d_pass.m5: h4. Now there are two passed pawns, one on the d-file and one on the h-file, far apart. The black king cannot hold both.
step.passMove: White to move and win. Pass the move, then collect the pawn.
step.passMove.hint: Don't move the king too soon: it is on its best square. Use the free pawn and, once the black king steps away, take the d5-pawn.
step.passMove.done: That's it. The pawn moved, the black king had to step away, and the d5-pawn fell. On the first move h3 worked too; Kf4 also won, but the pawn move is the simple way.
step.t_count: White to move. The same trébuchet, but now Black also has an h-pawn. Who wins here?
step.t_count.hint1: Count the pawn moves each side can still make before the h-pawns lock.
step.t_count.hint2: If each side answers the other's pawn move with a pawn move, who runs out first?
step.equal: Here the count is even: the h2-pawn and the h7-pawn share the same squares, h3, h4, h5 and h6. For each pawn move of mine, Black has an answer, and whoever moves first runs out first. With White to move, White loses. Spare tempi only count when one side has more than the other.
step.d_equal: Now with Black to move. The same count, but this time Black runs out.
step.d_equal.m1: Black spends a tempo. If Black played h5 at once, I would answer h4 and the pawns would lock with Black to move.
step.d_equal.m2: h3. I answer with one square. h4 here would be a mistake: Black would play h5 and make the last move.
step.d_equal.m4: h4. The pawns are locked, and the last pawn move was mine.
step.d_equal.m5: With no pawn moves left, the black king must step away.
step.d_equal.m6: Kxd5. The pawn falls and the game is won.
step.extra: Now White has two kingside pawns, g2 and h2, against one, h7. Both sides have tempi, but one has more. The side with more waiting pawn moves wins the fight. Just don't spend the wrong one: a pawn that can be captured doesn't pass the move.
step.extraMove: White to move and win. Spend the tempi one at a time, without leaving Black with the last one.
step.extraMove.hint: Answer each black pawn move with a pawn move of your own. Watch out for a pawn that steps onto a square where it can be taken.
step.extraMove.done: Well done. Black ran out of pawn moves first, and the black king has to drop the d5-pawn. After g3 h5, g4? lost: hxg4 and the tempo is gone.
step.t_double: White to move. The kings face each other with one square between them, and whoever has the move must give way. White has a pawn on c2, still on its starting square. How does White use that pawn?
step.t_double.hint1: You will need to pass the move more than once: now, and again when the king reaches e5.
step.t_double.hint2: A pawn on its starting square can move one square or two. How many waiting moves does it give in each case?
step.t_double.hint3: If the pawn jumps two squares at once, how many moves are left for later?
step.noReserve: First, the position without the c2-pawn. The kings are on e4 and e6, face to face, and White is to move: White has to retreat or step aside, and the black king advances. With no reserve, this position is lost for White. The c2-pawn is there to change that.
step.c4wrong: Now the tempting mistake: c4 straight away. It passes the move once, and Black answers with the king. But the pawn jumped two squares and has no move left. When my king reaches e5 and Black's goes to e7, White needs another waiting move and has none. It is a draw. The c2-pawn had two tempi, and c4 spent both at once.
step.d_double: The right way, one square at a time.
step.d_double.m1: c3! Just one square. The pawn passes the move and still keeps one move for later.
step.d_double.m2: The black king retreats. It has no better square.
step.d_double.m3: Ke5. My king advances, but the kings face each other again, and it is my move.
step.d_double.m4: The black king stands in front of mine. Without the second tempo, it would be a draw.
step.d_double.m5: c4! The pawn's second tempo. Now Black has to move.
step.d_double.m6: The black king steps aside and gives up the f6-square.
step.d_double.m7: Kf6. The king gets in and attacks the g6-pawn.
step.d_double.m8: The black king heads the other way. The g6-pawn has no defence left.
step.d_double.m9: Kxg6. The pawn falls, and my g5-pawn has a clear road.
step.doubleMove: White to move and win. Use the c2-pawn twice.
step.doubleMove.hint: Move the pawn just one square now, take the king to e5, and keep the other pawn move for when the kings face each other again.
step.doubleMove.done: Perfect: c3, the king to e5, and c4 at the moment it was needed. On the first move, Kf4 also won; c4? drew.
step.t_timing: White to move. The white king has not reached e5 yet. The h2-pawn is your reserve, and Black also has an h-pawn. What comes first: the king or the pawn?
step.t_timing.hint1: The h2-pawn can answer any move of the black pawn. Whoever spends first loses that edge.
step.t_timing.hint2: Take the king to the square where it attacks d5 and defends d4. The pawn waits.
step.early: See what happens if White plays h3 early. Black keeps his pawn back: the king goes to c4, my king goes to f4, Black plays h5, and when I reach e5 Black plays h4. The pawns are locked, the last move was Black's, and it is my turn: the trébuchet with White to move. White loses. The spare tempo was spent too soon.
step.d_timing.m1: Kf4! Only the king moves. The h2-pawn stays home, with both options.
step.d_timing.m2: The black king attacks d4 and defends d5.
step.d_timing.m3: Ke5. The trébuchet, with Black to move.
step.d_timing.m5: h4! Here the double step is right: the pawns lock with my move, and Black has none left.
step.d_timing.m6: The black king lets go of the d5-pawn.
step.d_timing.m7: Kxd5, the only winning move here. The pawn falls, and White has two pawns against one.
step.timingMove: White to move and win. The king first, the pawn at the end.
step.timingMove.hint: Don't touch the h2-pawn until the king reaches e5. It is your answer to the black pawn.
step.timingMove.done: That's it. The king reached e5 with the pawn still in reserve, and Black had to drop the d5-pawn. On the last move, h4 also won.
step.rules: Three rules. First: in a locked pawn ending, look for the zugzwangs; whoever has a pawn move to spare passes the move and wins. Second: count the pawn moves on both sides; if they are equal, the side to move runs out first. Third: keep your tempi for the end, and the pawn on its starting square for last, because it can choose between one square and two.
step.jump: One last thing about the double step. It is not always bad: it is a choice. Here the black pawn is already on h5, and only h4 locks the pawns with my move last. h3? would let Black play h4 and have the last move. Count first, then choose between one square and two.
step.jumpMove: White to move and win. One square or two?
step.jumpMove.hint: Count the empty squares between the h-pawns. You want to make the last pawn move.
step.jumpMove.done: That's it. h4 locked the pawns with my move, and then the king took the d5-pawn. There, Kxd5 was the only winning move.
step.finish: Now play it to the end. The white king is still on e3, the black king comes from the other side, and the computer defends Black as well as it can. Keep the h2-pawn for the right moment.
ex.e02: White to move and win. There is only one square between the h-pawns.
ex.e02.hint: Whoever takes the empty square between the pawns makes the last pawn move.
ex.e02.solution: h3! The pawns lock with your move, and Black, with no pawn move, must move the king. Every white king move loses.
ex.e08: White to move and win. Two pawns against one, with the black king stuck in the corner.
ex.e08.hint: The h2-pawn is your reserve. Keep its options open.
ex.e08.solution: g5 (h3 and Kh5 also win) and, after Kg8, h3!: the h-pawn moves one square at a time and keeps its tempi for the end. h4? at once draws, and on the second move only h3 wins.
ex.e10: White to move and win. A real, long ending: the first move decides.
ex.e10.hint: The b2-pawn has two tempi. You will need both later.
ex.e10.solution: Ke2! and Kd3!: the king advances and the b2-pawn stays home. b3? or b4? now draw; later, when the white king is close to the black one, the two tempi of the b-pawn decide.
ex.e11: White to move and win. Another zugzwang, this time on the queenside: the kings attack the b-pawns, and Black also has an h-pawn.
ex.e11.hint: The heart of the fight doesn't change: with the kings like this, whoever has the move loses. Count the empty squares between the h-pawns.
ex.e11.solution: h3! and, after h5, h4!: White makes the last pawn move, and the black king has to let go of the b5-pawn. h4? at once lost: Black answers h5 and keeps the last one. It is the same count as in the lesson, in a different structure.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Now White is the one defending, with one pawn against two.
ex.e12.hint: The h2-pawn is not for spending. Here the king does the waiting.
ex.e12.solution: Ke2! and, after h4, Kf2!: both are the only moves that hold. The king shuttles between e2 and f2 and the h2-pawn stays home: h3? or h4? lose at once. In defence the spare tempo counts too: spending it early hands the opponent the zugzwang he is looking for.
key.pass: The trébuchet with the h2-pawn: h3 or h4 passes the move and wins.
key.drmkc: From DrMkcTheHandsome's study: c3!, and c4 only when the king reaches e5.
history: Zugzwang is a German word meaning the compulsion to move. It already appeared in a German chess magazine in 1858, and in 1896 Friedrich Amelung also used Tempozwang, the compulsion to spend a tempo. In pawn endings the idea got a name of its own: the reserve tempo, a pawn move kept back to pass the move. In 1986 Klaus Bischoff resigned against John Nunn in a position where White's a-pawn was still on its starting square: moving one square or two, as needed, it put Black in zugzwang. Max Euwe and David Hooper, in their 1959 guide to endings, already showed a position where a single tempo decided: whoever had the move won. Mark Dvoretsky gave the theme a whole section in the pawn-endings chapter of his manual.
practice: Now the two-tempo ending for real, as a practical test. c3 first, the king forward, and c4 at the right moment. Pick the time control and go.
